reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is primarily an instructional walkthrough of eBay seller-account restrictions, support navigation, and visible eBay support pages. Although it includes typed identity and account details, discussion of opening another account, ambiguous discount wording, and a subscription request, these cues do not establish impersonation, submitted information, a deceptive transaction, or a supported link to financial participation.

opening.argument: The video links a concrete financial benefit to a purchase action: viewers are told to buy products from a dollar site, then shown a deal in which they can buy for $299 and take $180. That is not merely neutral account education; it presents an unusually favorable outcome alongside an action a viewer can take. The surrounding instructions also direct viewers toward a tool for checking the discounted price, making the benefit operational rather than hypothetical. The offer is therefore framed as an easy acquisition opportunity tied to buying.

citations.quote: you need to buy these products from the dollar site with this discounted discount
if you want to see the discount price in this tool you can check the $189 with this deal
You can buy $299 and take $ 180 when you buy it

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the video an account-support walkthrough does not explain away the separate purchase-and-benefit pitch. The title identifies account restrictions, but the narration also tells viewers to buy products and describes taking $180 from a $299 purchase. The presence of help-page navigation cannot establish that the deal is genuine or harmless.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted purchase language does not establish a guaranteed reward, a required payment to access a withdrawal, or a deceptive transaction. It appears in a confused discussion of product pricing and discounts, while the central walkthrough concerns account support. The evidence shows a stated deal, not that viewers were promised cash or induced into a scam flow.

opening.argument: Several genuine warning signals appear together: a claimed eBay contact channel, requests for account and identity information, and instructions connected to suspended accounts. The video says viewers should provide an account number, phone number, address, and account ID card, while the screen shows a message headed by an eBay contact and asks for identifying details. It also discusses opening another account with new details after suspension. Even if each item can have an innocent reading, this combination creates a high-risk pathway for collecting sensitive information while presenting account access and favorable deals as attainable.

citations.quote: When you start speaking, you should tell him about the account number, which was already registered on that site
After you have to enter your account's ID card to do so
Then, you should open a new account and put the details there and run the program

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats the visible support page as authentication, but a support interface does not prove that the person or contact receiving the requested information is authorized. The material expressly asks for account-identifying data and separately discusses using new details after suspension. Those are risk signals the general label of 'walkthrough' leaves unresolved.

citations.quote: After you have to enter your account's ID card to do so
Do not use some new details Use new details and new details

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The screen and narration do not show that any viewer submitted data, that the contact was fraudulent, or that the information led to money or account access. The account-ID language can be read as troubleshooting identity verification, and the account-creation discussion is unclear and inconsistent. Suspicious possibility is not proof of the low-barrier reward category.

opening.argument: The educational framing functions as promotion because the video repeatedly steers viewers toward the channel, contact channels, tools, and account actions rather than simply explaining policy. It asks viewers to subscribe, directs them to help and contact options, gives a phone-contact process, and then adds purchase discounts and product-buying instructions. The channel description also supplies Instagram, Facebook, and channel links. Taken together, the supposed tutorial builds an audience and routes viewers toward participation while presenting easy account recovery and deal-related activity.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference opening narrows the video to support navigation and overlooks how the presenter converts that topic into audience and participation prompts. Subscription, external social links, phone contact, and a stated purchase discount are not needed to demonstrate an eBay help page. The instructional wrapper therefore also serves a promotional function.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promotion of a YouTube channel or social pages does not establish a scam reward, and a subscription request is not a payment or investment instruction. The purchase language is confusing and lacks a demonstrated claim that viewers would receive money. The central visible and narrated activity remains support navigation, including an option to ask for help and contact.
